segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: A quick warning that if you're squeamish or averse to graphic images of food, there's going to be some of that in this report. Here's Ben Calhoun.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: I first heard about this whole thing in an email. It came from a listener, a woman named Emily Rancer. She works in the food industry.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: And the letter Emily wrote was about a story she'd heard from a farmer. The farmer who told her this is apparently a person of some standing in the pork industry. And admittedly, I don't know the first thing about the pork industry, but he's in charge of a pork-producing operation that spans several states.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: The story he told Emily went something like this, a while ago, he was visiting a pork processing plant in Oklahoma. He's walking through it with a friend, a guy who managed the plant, actually. And at some point, he saw boxes stacked on the floor, labeled "artificial calamari."

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: He stood there, wondering for a second. And then he asked his friend, what's artificial calamari? Bung, his friend replied. It's hog rectum, rectum that would be sliced into rings, deep fried, and boom, there you have it.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: OK, if I can, let me just narrate for you what this would mean. It would mean that in restaurants everywhere, right this second, people are squeezing lemon wedges over crispy, golden rings, and dipping the rings into marinara sauce, and they're eating hog rectum.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: Now, they're chewing, satisfied, and deeply clueless. It's payback. It's payback for our blissful ignorance about where our food comes from and how it gets to us. It's amazing. And it's perfect.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: But it also seems like it couldn't possibly be true. So I called up the farmer to talk to him personally. I wanted to hear it firsthand. And the farmer confirmed the story-- the entire thing, the boxes, the bung. But when I asked him to go on the record, to tape an interview, and gave his name here, on the radio, he very politely declined, which seems suspicious, right?

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: When I asked him why, he said he'd spoken with his girlfriend about it, and she suggested that he should think about the words that he wanted to come up when somebody Googled his name. This was all fine, though, because he referred me to the real expert, the guy who gave him the tour of the hog processing plant. And that guy, he agreed to talk.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: [PHONE RINGING]

segments.speaker: Ron Meek
segments.text: Hello.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: Hi, is this Ron?

segments.speaker: Ron Meek
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: Yeah, this is Ron Meek, meat processing plant manager, presently residing in Mountain View, Missouri, where he runs an organic beef processing plant there called Beyond Organic. If the story really were true, Ron would have been the guy who explained to the farmer what was in those boxes.

segments.speaker: Ron Meek
segments.text: The boxes are 10-pound boxes, and they were all-- they cut off so much of it, maybe a 10- or 12-inch piece of the bung. And you know what it looks like? This looks like, after they're cleaned and washed and everything, they just look like a bunch of big noodles in a box, is all it looks like.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: But specifically, the labels that said "imitation calamari," where did you personally see the "imitation calamari?"

segments.speaker: Ron Meek
segments.text: Oh, I've seen a label say that. That's all I was told by the people that told me that. The people I work for, they told me that.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: Oh, the people that you worked for told you that it was used for imitation calamari?

segments.speaker: Ron Meek
segments.text: Right.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: And is there any possibility that you think that when they were explaining this to you, that they were kind of having you on a little bit?

segments.speaker: Ron Meek
segments.text: Having me on?

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: Yeah, like--

segments.speaker: Ron Meek
segments.text: Bull-[BLEEP] me?

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Ron Meek
segments.text: Well, I wouldn't think that. But it could be 5%. It could have been that. But I seriously doubt it.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: OK, just to give a little better picture, a pork bung-- and "bung" is the actual industry term for it-- is long and floppy and ugly. At one end, it widens out into this more bulbous shape, like a pink, wrinkly pear. That's the rectum. At the other end, it narrows into a soft, pinkish-white tube.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: I know, it sounds gross. But also, consider, we are a nation that eats more than a billion pounds of sausage every year, billion with a B. Maybe you like liverwurst or capicola or summer sausage with a natural casing. Then you, like me, have eaten bung-- stuffed, dried bung.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: A lot of brats and Italian sausages are stuffed in intestine. So if you eat those regularly, you pretty much live up the street from bung. So why does the idea of a fried ring of bung just feel grosser? Well, partly, it's the visual, right? When you see that little ring of calamari, you don't want to picture it in the context of a pig's behind.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: Then there are all the people who don't eat pork, period. Ron said there's also another reason.

segments.speaker: Ron Meek
segments.text: Just because of the word "bung," probably. I mean, people don't just want to jump up and say, man, I'm going to eat me some bung tonight. I mean, that's just the way it is.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: But the big question, the question you've been thinking about since we got on this topic, have you or I eaten imitation calamari, bung dressed up as seafood? Well, Ron didn't know. He said his plant exported a lot of their bung to Asia. But he just didn't know much about whatever happened after it left the door. So he could only speculate. Anything, he said, would be a wild guess.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: So I turned to people who would know. Is pork bung being falsely peddled as calamari? I called the USDA. The USDA's Food Inspection Service issued the following statement to me. "Products we inspect, including those derived from pork, must be accurately labeled and cannot purport to be a product of another species."

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: So it's against the rules. But people break the rules. A recent study of seafood by a group called Oceana used DNA testing, and found that all across the country, fish is regularly being labeled as other species in restaurants and in grocery stores, escolar sold as white tuna, Pacific rockfish being fraudulently sold as snapper.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: In Miami, more than 30% of fish was being sold as something it wasn't. In New York, the number was 39%, Boston, 48%, Los Angeles-- are you ready? 55%, 55. That means if you order fish in LA, you are most likely eating a species you did not order.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: In other words, seafood substitution is rampant in this country. And depending on where you live, from what I can tell, you can get cleaned hog bung for about half the price of clean squid. So there would be money in it if you could pull off the switch. And as best as I can tell, were you to do this, you would not be caught.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: A lawyer who's familiar with this area of law and regulation told me, once bung leaves the plant, there's a variety of agencies and entities that would be in play-- USDA, FDA, state, and local government. But ultimately, he said, the regulation we have is not designed to catch an offense like this. It's aimed mostly at sanitation and food safety.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: So bottom line, the lawyer said, if somebody wanted to do it, chances are, they'd get away with it. So is someone out there doing this? Well, for weeks, I looked for an answer. The USDA says they've never heard of anyone trying to pass pork bung as squid or any other species.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: [PHONE RINGING]

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: I contacted the National Restaurant Association, the National Pork Producers Council, the National Pork Board--

segments.speaker: Woman On Phone
segments.text: Hello?

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: --a squid fisherman's association--

segments.speaker: Woman On Phone
segments.text: Good afternoon.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: --Cisco and other big food and restaurant supply companies.

segments.speaker: Woman On Phone
segments.text: It's hog what?

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: Bung, hog rectum.

segments.speaker: Woman On Phone
segments.text: Oh, my gosh.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: That's the executive director of the California Wet Fish Producers Association. But the answer was pretty much always the same, nobody had heard of it. But almost to a person, they added that that doesn't mean it's not happening somewhere.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: Ron Meeks said a lot of the bung from his plant got exported. So my next call was to the US Meat Export Federation, which confirmed that, quote, "the main destinations for pork bungs are China, Hong Kong, Japan, Taiwan, Korea, and the Philippines. They are mainly used for processing. But we are aware of some uses in soups and certain entrees. We are not aware of them being used as a substitute for calamari, but it's not impossible," unquote.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: So over the past few weeks, I've called Asian food suppliers, people who live in, work in, and eat in those countries. I talked to a woman named Corinne Trang, who's written an overarching compendium of Asian cuisines. I've talked to academics at NYU and Haverford and USC and Harvard. I've reached out to chefs who know Asian food.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: The answer, again, always similar-- never heard of it, but it's possible, partly because bung doesn't have such a complicated reputation in Asia, where it has to be some kind of secret ingredient, like it does here. On the other hand, though, people pointed out that in Korea and Japan, you can't get more than a few hours from the ocean. Squid is cheap and it's readily available. You'd only eat a substitute if you wanted the substitute.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: Generally, people said, if the switch was happening somewhere, they'd guess China. Eventually, I found my way to this guy, who I was really excited about, someone who I thought might have my answer. He was, get this, an anthropologist who lived and worked in China for 40 years, where he studied food, and specifically, meat.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: When I talked to him, though, he made two points. Point one, my question about this happening in Asia was racist. Even just asking the question was racist because it plays on ignorant stereotypes about other cultures eating things that we perceive as weird. Point two was that Ron Meek, my guy from the pig plant, Ron was pulling my leg. And he was getting away with it because I was a dumbass.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: He told me more than once that I should, quote, "find something worthwhile to do with myself." When we ended our conversation, he told me that he was refusing to even dignify what I was doing by appearing on the radio or by letting me use his name.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: OK, so to respond to his points one by one, first, am I racist against Asians? Well, I'm half Chinese. My mom's Chinese. Like anyone, I've had the occasional issue with my mother. But this has not been one of them. We grew up eating chicken feet and fish eyes. And I think it's possible to raise the question of who eats what without being racist.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: His second point, though, that Ron Meek was pulling my leg, I mean, the guy was still an expert on meat in China. So I called Ron back.

segments.speaker: Ron Meek
segments.text: All right, shoot me some questions, dude.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: I told him the whole thing, about the anthropologist, about what he said.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: I guess, I mean, the only thing I want to ask you is, are you messing with me?

segments.speaker: Ron Meek
segments.text: No. I mean, that was what my boss told me. I was like, what the hell do we save these hog bungs for? He says they use them for imitation squids and stuff like that.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: So in your heart of hearts, you believe it?

segments.speaker: Ron Meek
segments.text: Yeah, man, I mean, I ain't going to sit here and tell you things that, they're just bull-[BLEEP], and play with you, when I'm just going off of my knowledge of saving hog bungs. I mean, you got to think about how far advanced slaughterhouses are, especially big ones, that want to make every penny count.

segments.speaker: Ron Meek
segments.text: The one I worked at, you bring the pigs in, you stun them, then you stick them, and the blood goes off into a trough, and it goes down. And it's vacuum sucked out of there with a vacuum, into centrifuges. And they separate the blood from the blood plasma. And they save that.

segments.speaker: Ron Meek
segments.text: I mean, they save the lungs. They save the pancreas. They save the spleens. They save the hearts. The only thing left, by the time it's all said and done, is a skull and jawbones. I mean, you can be an anthropologist all you want. And if you don't work in a processing plant, you don't know [BLEEP].

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: I contacted the plant Ron worked at, where this happened. And for what it's worth, they backed him up. They said their sales team had heard of people eating pork bung as imitation calamari, though they hadn't witnessed it firsthand or heard it directly from a customer. It was all hearsay.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: So at the end of all this, I still had no proof that anyone was passing off bung as squid. And then I realized I hadn't asked the more basic question here. Could bung do it? Could it pass as calamari? And that question led me to a guy named Eddie Lin. Eddie Lin has eaten a lot of bung, at least a hundred times, he said, probably more. Eddie has an extreme food blog called "Deep-End Dining" and an online TV show called Kamikaze Kitchen.

segments.speaker: Eddie Lin
segments.text: I can definitely see a resemblance, texture-wise.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: Oh, really?

segments.speaker: Eddie Lin
segments.text: Yeah, yeah, definitely. There's a rubbery texture, sort of like a calamari.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: Huh.

segments.speaker: Eddie Lin
segments.text: But you would really have to get rid of that, needless to say, foul flavor and odor from the bung.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: Somehow, I hadn't figured that the bung, once it was scrubbed and rinsed and cleaned with steam, that it would still taste like, you know.

segments.speaker: Eddie Lin
segments.text: So yeah, you would definitely have to do some major, major blanching-- or brining. I meant brining.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: Uh-huh, to just to try and leach those flavors out of there?

segments.speaker: Eddie Lin
segments.text: Yeah, I mean, those flavors have been marinating in that pig for quite a while. So--

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: A lifetime?

segments.speaker: Eddie Lin
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Eddie Lin
segments.text: [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: He thought it wouldn't be easy, but he thought it could be done. And there was only one way to tell if he was right, to cook up some bung and eat it. And if the taste was overwhelming and the texture was all wrong, well, then I'd have my answer. And at this point, I'll be frank, I started to root for the bung.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: I realized that this is not a story about fraud. It's not a bait-and-switch story. It's a story about possibility. It's classic rags to riches. It's about whether a cut of meat, perhaps the lowliest, most malignable cut of meat in America, might somehow, in at least one place on the planet, be dipped in the redemptive oils of the great culinary equalizer that is the deep fryer. And it might emerge transformed, no longer an outcast, but instead, hair combed, clean-shaven, in a suit and tie. It might walk reborn onto a table.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: Through sheer force of resemblance, it might be loved, its history, years of drudgery and hardship, doing the body's least glamorous job, all washed away. No, this is not the story of a con man like Bernie Madoff. It's Pretty Woman. This is whether Good Will Hunting finds his way out of Southie. It's whether Charlie, on that very last chocolate bar, really can get a golden ticket.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: To do all this, to try it, I called my little sister, Lauren. She's a chef, trained abroad at The Cordon Bleu, worked at Michelin-star restaurants. She's that kind of chef. Soon, we were standing in front of a deli case. And I don't know why I feel hesitant about saying this because I don't think it's racist. It was in Chinatown.

segments.speaker: Lauren
segments.text: Pork bung, there it is. Look at it, it looks like a sphincter.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: Wait, what do you mean, it looks like a--

segments.speaker: Lauren
segments.text: This one up here, that's cut up, it looks like a butt hole.

segments.speaker: Lauren
segments.text: [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: It does.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And Lauren had theories about pulling it off-- brining, soaking, maybe braising. But once we got to the store, once she'd seen the meat up close, her doubts got worse.

segments.speaker: Lauren
segments.text: I think, after looking at it, I don't think it's going to--

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: You don't think it's going to work?

segments.speaker: Lauren
segments.text: No. It's too thick. There's too much muscle tissue. It's too thick. You'd have to use a ring cutter to make it the right thickness.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: What do you think those bits are, in there?

segments.speaker: Lauren
segments.text: Oh, you know, poo.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: My sister said Eddie Lin was definitely right. The giveaway would be the stubborn flavor of poo. That flavor, she said, it's tough to get rid of. The Earth revolves around the sun. And bung will always taste like [BLEEP].

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: But there was no backing out now. We would eat. We would eat our way to the truth. And so what if it didn't look good? So what if bung was destined to taste like bung? You know who it didn't look good for, and he still put up a fight? Rocky Balboa, that's who. This was it, the bung versus calamari, squid versus tail, The Rumble in the Bunghole.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: We set up the tasting at a restaurant, in the lull between lunch and dinner. In the dining room, there was just a few tables eating. And all around the restaurant, the morning shift was wrapping up as we walked in with a red cooler filled with squid and hog bung.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: So originally, I'd recruited some half a dozen people from our office at This American Life as tasters. The final group the day of the tasting included, from the office, Seth Lind and Brian Reed.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: So when's the last time that you guys had calamari?

segments.speaker: Seth Lind
segments.text: I had calamari probably a month ago.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: And what about you, Brian?

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: I haven't had it since we got this tip about the possible--

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: Oh, my gosh, have you been avoiding?

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: Yeah, no, totally. And to be honest, I ate calamari pretty regular. I'm a regular eater of calamari-- not all the time, but it's something I'll routinely order if it's on an appetizer menu.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: I mean, I grew up in an Italian-American family, where my grandparents were also born here. I feel like calamari is just big among that sector of people, at Olive Garden and stuff like that. So I just grew up eating it.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: I hadn't realized this. For weeks, Brian had been avoiding calamari. He'd been living in fear.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: Brian, if you find out that they're indiscernible from each other, will you ever eat calamari again?

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: No, I don't think so. That's why I want to do this, just to know, going forward.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: Back in the kitchen, things were looking bad. I'd given up on the idea that bung would taste the same as calamari. Now I'd hung my hopes on the idea that at least visually, it would look the same. But as my sister dropped the flowered rings of hog bung into the fryer, they had turned into this kind of big, ugly, tangled wad, nothing like the jiggly squid rings.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: Oh, they're very scraggly-looking.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But then, as if by a miracle, they changed. My sister gave a shake to the fry basket, and as they sizzled, the bung just seemed to gracefully snap into rings.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: Oh, look at that, though. It's like magic. They're turning into circles.

segments.speaker: Lauren
segments.text: Yeah. So I'm going to pull these first ones.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: Soon, we were face to face with the plate. On it, there were two piles of rings, similar in size, similar in shape. The bung had more of a frizzly edge to it, kind of like a fancy onion ring. The calamari was smoother.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: OK, so--

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I asked Seth and Brian to just give a first impression.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: I have a guess. But it's one of those things where you're pretty sure, but you could totally be wrong.

segments.speaker: Seth Lind
segments.text: God, I thought I would be more sure. I don't-- I'm waffling now. My gut reaction is that this was calamari and this was not.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: OK, before you eat it, see, I totally thought this was calamari, the other one.

segments.speaker: Seth Lind
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: So I'm going to do it at the same time.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: OK, so just to be clear what's going on here, Seth has chosen one pile of rings which he thinks is calamari. Brian has done the same thing, only Brian is choosing the other stack of fried rings.

segments.speaker: Seth Lind
segments.text: OK, so we're about to bite into these simultaneously, which we both think this is calamari.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: But they're the opposite ones.

segments.speaker: Seth Lind
segments.text: The opposite ones. OK.

segments.speaker: Seth Lind
segments.text: [CRUNCHING]

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: So in actuality, Seth is right. Seth is eating calamari. The chewing you hear from Brian's mic, that is the sound of a calamari lover eating fried pig rectum. I should also add there were actually two varieties of bung on the plate that day, one bung that my sister had blanched over and over to mellow any organ-y, fecal flavor, and then untreated, straight-up bung, unfiltered, unchained, uncut, 100% pure bung. That one, the latter one, bung at its purest, at the height of its bunginess, this is what Brian was eating. As they ate, Seth still looked confident.

segments.speaker: Seth Lind
segments.text: I think I was right.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: (LAUGHING) I think I was right.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: Really?

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: Yeah. I totally think I was right.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: Game, set, match, bung. And it wasn't just Brian. I thought so. Damien, who manages the restaurant, he also thought it was passable. A few of us picked up a faint flavor of pork rind, but if you weren't really looking for it, you wouldn't notice it was there. One of the restaurant staff, a guy named Ethan Vanburen, had the simplest, clearest explanation.

segments.speaker: Ethan Vanburen
segments.text: I think that when you slice something up really thin and deep fry it, it's going to taste like something that's been deep fried.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: If a plate full of the bung came out, how many people do you think would even-- do you think you'd notice if you were in that setting?

segments.speaker: Ethan Vanburen
segments.text: I'd say top scenario is somebody says, this calamari tastes funny, and keeps eating it.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: And as for Brian-- oh, Brian-- Brian was reeling a bit, trying to figure out just what this was going to mean for him.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: I'm sure I've been fooled in the past. I'm just, like, sure of it.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: Wait, oh, you're thinking that you've been places in the past, and you've had bung?

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: I just imagined seeing a plate with this food, that looks like this on it, sitting with my family, growing up. We definitely have eaten something that tasted like this, and just thought it was calamari, for sure.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: Not only wasn't he sure if he'd ever eat calamari again, he didn't want to eat the calamari on the plate in front of him, calamari I guaranteed him, was real.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: Just to repeat one last time, I have no proof that anyone, anywhere, has ever tried to pass off pork bung as calamari in a restaurant. All I know is, if you wanted to do it, it would be easy. And I'm choosing to believe that it's happening somewhere, because at some point in working on this story, I stopped identifying with Brian and anyone who might feel ripped off or grossed out by getting imitation instead of the real thing.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: Now, I identify with the bung. I'd like to think that somewhere out there, right now, under a heat lamp, a platter is sitting. It's warm, and it's full of promise and transformation and redemption. That's the world that I'll choose to live in for me, for you, for the bung. For the bung in all of us.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Ben Calhoun, he's one of the producers of our program.

segments.speaker: Fred Armisen
segments.text: (IMITATING IRA GLASS) Ben Calhoun, he's one of the producers of our program. Thanks to the restaurant Aurora, in Brooklyn, for letting us use their kitchen for our taste test.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Fred Armisen
segments.text: (IMITATING IRA GLASS) OK, who is this? Wait, who am I?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Well, coming up, Philadelphia and Afghanistan, doppelgangers?

segments.speaker: Fred Armisen
segments.text: (IMITATING IRA GLASS) That's in a minute. From Chicago Public Radio and Public Radio International, when our program continues.

segments.speaker: Fred Armisen
segments.text: (IMITATING IRA GLASS) So we're going to start act 2?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Start here. So we're coming back from the ID break.

segments.speaker: Fred Armisen
segments.text: (IMITATING IRA GLASS) It's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. Each week on our show, of course, we choose a theme. We bring you different kinds of stories on that theme. Today's show, doppelgangers, stories of things that have a double, an evil twin, or a not-so-evil twin.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Oh, wait, I should just explain. Oh, right, so--

segments.speaker: Fred Armisen
segments.text: (IMITATING IRA GLASS) What?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: That was just a note to myself. I should explain.

segments.speaker: Fred Armisen
segments.text: (IMITATING IRA GLASS) No, that was a note to me.

segments.speaker: Fred Armisen
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So this is why Fred is here. Fred Armisen is co-hosting the show as me because it's a show about doubles and lookalikes.

segments.speaker: Fred Armisen
segments.text: (IMITATING IRA GLASS) Right, but we're both creating the same person, in a sense. And that's what the fun is of--

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Oh, that was really good, the way you just did that.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Finish your thought.

segments.speaker: Fred Armisen
segments.text: I didn't have an end to that thought. I just--

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: You just knew that--

segments.speaker: Fred Armisen
segments.text: I like when you do the little self-- the little discovery.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: All right, well, we have arrived at Act 2 of our program, Act 2, In Country and City. So for decades now, the writer Alex Kotlowitz has been writing about the inner cities, and especially the toll of violence on young people. He's probably best known for his book, There Are No Children Here. He appears on our show from time to time.

segments.speaker: Fred Armisen
segments.text: (IMITATING IRA GLASS) Recently, he heard about an unusual program at Drexel University in Philadelphia, where they're giving guys from inner city neighborhoods counseling for symptoms of PTSD.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And this interested Alex, because for a long time, he has wondered whether the violence that he was reporting on in Chicago and its effect on kids and adults was comparable to the effects of trauma that a person experiences at war.

segments.speaker: Fred Armisen
segments.text: (IMITATING IRA GLASS) So he knew, and we know, how strange that sounds, to compare being in Afghanistan or Iraq to working a street corner in Chicago or some other city.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So Alex tried to see if it was really comparable by doing a pair of interviews. He talked to this vet from Afghanistan and also a guy from Philadelphia, who's lived in some pretty bad neighborhoods his whole life. Alex wanted to see if they were doubles of some kind for each other.

segments.speaker: Fred Armisen
segments.text: (IMITATING IRA GLASS) One of these guys is 28, one is 30, and both of them are trying to make sense of what they experienced. Here's Alex.

segments.speaker: Alex Kotlowitz
segments.text: Here's the first of these two guys, Brandon Caro. Brandon spent a year in Afghanistan. His roughest time was the six months he spent in the eastern part of the country, near the Pakistani border. He was a Navy corpsman, a medic who worked with the Marines.

segments.speaker: Brandon Caro
segments.text: As a teenager, yeah, I certainly lacked discipline. I had been thrown out of my house more times than I can remember. And I was 21 when I enlisted. And really, I enlisted because I had, up to that point, not finished college. And it didn't seem as though I was going to finish college any time soon.

segments.speaker: Alex Kotlowitz
segments.text: Then there's Curtis Jefferson. He grew up in a rough neighborhood in North Philly, where he oversaw a small group of guys who sold drugs. He made his first drug sale when he was still in high school.

segments.speaker: Curtis Jefferson
segments.text: I was 16. My aunt gave me some money for school. And that point, I purchased some weed and some crack with that, never bought my clothes. After that, I sold all the drugs. And I guess from there, that's where it started. I seen that money come in, and I wasn't asking nobody for no money. Especially with my aunt, I wasn't begging for from her pockets and all that. So from there, it was all she wrote.

segments.speaker: Alex Kotlowitz
segments.text: OK, they're two completely different people who made very different choices in their lives. But I spoke to each of them, looking for similarities in their experiences. And honestly, there were more than I expected. Here's the first similarity.

segments.speaker: Alex Kotlowitz
segments.text: For Curtis on the street, and for Brandon in Afghanistan, they could never let their guard down. During his tour, Brandon was charged with training Afghan soldiers. And in May 2007, he heard about Afghan soldiers who attacked their American trainers.

segments.speaker: Brandon Caro
segments.text: They had weapons around us all the time. On convoys, we would have to line him up in the morning and collect their cell phones because we couldn't trust them not to inform on us to Taliban fighters. It was exhausting, trying to keep an eye on the Afghan soldiers and look out for IEDs or snipers.

segments.speaker: Curtis Jefferson
segments.text: Because you're trying to focus on one thing, you're trying to get money, but the same thing, eventually, somebody's going to come up and test you. Somebody's going to test you. Somebody's going to rob you. Somebody's going to send something to your boys, they're going to get robbed. Somebody's going to send shots your way or something.

segments.speaker: Brandon Caro
segments.text: It felt like a piano could fall on you at any time. That's what it felt like to be on patrol, and especially to be on patrol with the Afghans.

segments.speaker: Curtis Jefferson
segments.text: Because when you're out there, you notice different things-- for one, people with their hands in their pockets.

segments.speaker: Brandon Caro
segments.text: You're looking for someone that doesn't look right, that doesn't feel right.

segments.speaker: Curtis Jefferson
segments.text: Another thing, people who've got hoodies on, especially black. There's a certain look, put the hoodie on their face, you can't even see their eyeballs. Come on, it's daytime. I can't see your face. Let me see your eyes or something.

segments.speaker: Brandon Caro
segments.text: And I would watch the way they looked at me, If they would stare back at me, if they would smile at me.

segments.speaker: Curtis Jefferson
segments.text: If a person always got to keep touching their side, you're not going in your pocket, you're touching something. And I've been out there so long, I could tell if somebody's got a gun on them or not.

segments.speaker: Brandon Caro
segments.text: For some reason, it was always a white Toyota Camry that was packed with explosives and driven into a convoy, or driven into a checkpoint.

segments.speaker: Curtis Jefferson
segments.text: Grand Marquis, or what else? Crown Victoria, that's a dope-boy car. When I seen them cars when I was on the streets, it was either get ready, go for the straps, go to the guns, or get out of the way. That might be the hop-out boys, come stick you up.

segments.speaker: Alex Kotlowitz
segments.text: Here's something else they shared. They both saw people killed, and then had to figure out how to keep going. The first fatality Brandon ever saw came when a convoy, which he was originally scheduled to be a part of, was hit.

segments.speaker: Brandon Caro
segments.text: They brought the casualties into our base. And when we swung open the two doors that opened up into the cab of the truck, I was looking at just a heap, a mass of flesh, and that gray, digital-pattern Army uniform. But there was no form to what I was looking at. I knew that what I was looking at was human. But I didn't know what position the body was in because it had been so badly damaged.

segments.speaker: Brandon Caro
segments.text: And so we got into the cab and we started to put him into a bag. And I tried not to look at his face. I remember thinking, don't look at his face, don't look at his face. But I had to, inevitably. It was by far, the most intimate, goriest thing I've ever experienced in my life.

segments.speaker: Curtis Jefferson
segments.text: My first time seeing somebody shot was my own mother. I was five years old, going on six. We were living in the projects, Blumberg projects. My mom, she just got her degree in nursing. She was a nurse, had a nice little job. She was working to get us out of the projects.

segments.speaker: Curtis Jefferson
segments.text: Then one morning, she was going out to work, gave my mom a kiss on the lips, and she told my grandma, I'll see y'all later. I'm going to work. As soon as she went out to work, I just heard all this shooting. By that time, I knew what shooting was. But there it was. She just got caught up in a shootout.

segments.speaker: Curtis Jefferson
segments.text: Somebody knocked on the door. She told my grandma, she said, Barbara's laying on the ground. All I know is my grandma was screaming and hollering. And she ran outside. And there she was, right on the ground, just red blood, just nothing but blood.

segments.speaker: Curtis Jefferson
segments.text: Just looking at it her, I'm five years old, like, what's wrong with Mommy, Grandma? What's wrong with her? My grandma's crying and screaming. She didn't even say nothing. She just keep telling me, go in the house, go in the house, go in the house.

segments.speaker: Curtis Jefferson
segments.text: I was angry a lot, every day, every day, because I thought about my mom, every day, every day, every day. I still think about her every day.

segments.speaker: Brandon Caro
segments.text: From that point on, it was very difficult for me to sleep, to focus. I didn't realize how much those things really had made an impact on me, but they did.

segments.speaker: Curtis Jefferson
segments.text: I seen a lot of people get shot. I seen people get shot by cops. And I seen best friends shoot each other. I seen all types of crazy stuff. I don't know.

segments.speaker: Brandon Caro
segments.text: There was a convoy that went up to Naray, in which there was a sniper attack that killed my old sergeant and his sergeant. There was the rocket-propelled grenade attack on a tent, inside our FOB, followed up by machine-gun fire.

segments.speaker: Curtis Jefferson
segments.text: [SIGHS] I could say I had seen a dozen. And for me to not even be like no cop or no doctor or nothing, that's a whole lot to see somebody killed and dead. That's a whole lot.

segments.speaker: Alex Kotlowitz
segments.text: This brings us to the third parallel, they buried their feelings.

segments.speaker: Curtis Jefferson
segments.text: Well, after my mom got shot, I didn't get no counseling. I didn't get no counselor at all. And my aunt asked me, too. My aunt gave me a decision. And she asked me one day. I had to have been, like, 12. She was like, do you want to go to counseling? And I told her, no, for what? I don't need to talk to nobody. I was so much in denial. I think I can handle everything by myself, but I really couldn't.

segments.speaker: Brandon Caro
segments.text: I think at that point, I was probably still in denial. I knew that I was toting around a lot of emotional baggage. As much as I wanted to talk to people about how I really felt, I also didn't want to talk about it at all. The more I'd give it air, the more real it would be. And I didn't want it to be real. I just wanted it to be over.

segments.speaker: Curtis Jefferson
segments.text: I can't show no weakness because, you know what I mean? My homies need me out there. And I've been doing that for years. It's to the point, I started getting adapted to it, like, [BLEEP]. But at the same time, I was still scared. Don't nobody want to die like that.

segments.speaker: Alex Kotlowitz
segments.text: The fourth shared experience-- raw, unfiltered rage.

segments.speaker: Curtis Jefferson
segments.text: I was definitely looking for revenge for my mom. When I was about 10 years old, I told my aunt I was going to look for the people that killed my mom. And I was going to go back down to the projects, and I was going to kill them. I always thought like that.

segments.speaker: Brandon Caro
segments.text: I mean, the way I felt about the Afghans, I began to just hate that whole culture, entirely. I hated them. There was one time, we were driving on an extremely, extremely dangerous road. And we had come very close to falling off the cliff, which would have killed us.

segments.speaker: Brandon Caro
segments.text: And the truck to our front was a truck filled with Afghan soldiers. And they were pointing and laughing at us for almost falling off. And in that moment, more than any other moment, I wanted to open up on them and kill every one of them. I've realized how much anger and resentment I have, and how dangerous that is.

segments.speaker: Curtis Jefferson
segments.text: Man, I shot my sister's boyfriend. I mean, he-- I don't know, I think I had one of them moments. It had to have been, because it just took one word, and it just set me off for no reason, just thinking about everything. And I just shot him.

segments.speaker: Curtis Jefferson
segments.text: I felt some type of way. I made the situation deeper, and it wasn't. You know what I mean? It wasn't even that deep. But I've been holding a lot of stuff in, because he was always trying to discipline me. That's what it was, I didn't like about it, how he always tried to discipline me.

segments.speaker: Curtis Jefferson
segments.text: All my sisters are way older than me, they're 40, pushing 50. See what I'm saying? I'm the youngest. And I'm the only boy. So her boyfriends, they're just, oh, you need to stop getting the streets. But it's just how he was saying it. Don't raise your voice at me. He's talking about, yeah, I'm going to take you in the street and fight you and all this. You're going to learn your lesson.

segments.speaker: Curtis Jefferson
segments.text: It just was the part where he was like, yeah, I'm going to knock you the [BLEEP] out. And that just went in my head, like, what? First thing I do is grab my gun and come around the corner. And he was outside, too. And I'm thinking the whole time, I hope he ain't really outside. So he thinks I'm going to fight him. I'm not fighting this man. I'm going to kill him.

segments.speaker: Curtis Jefferson
segments.text: I didn't even give him a chance to put his hands up. As soon as I got around there, he was just all in my face, and just backed up and shot him, shot him in the stomach. I thought I was going to kill him. I thought he was dead, though. I guess everything worked out in its ways. He's ain't a person to tell-- he ain't tell. He still survived, so I don't know.

segments.speaker: Alex Kotlowitz
segments.text: Here's something I didn't expect with either of them. The toughest times weren't when they were on the battlefield or in the streets. It was when things were quiet. That's when they struggled the most.

segments.speaker: Brandon Caro
segments.text: The worst times, for me, were the times where we weren't out on patrol, because that's when I was alone with my thoughts. And I would try to clear my head. It was impossible. These thoughts would just appear. I would worry. I thought about what it would be like to be shot.

segments.speaker: Curtis Jefferson
segments.text: I might daydream, just look at my ceiling or something, watch TV, like, damn, just imagine bullets going, ripping through my body. You know, mother-[BLEEP] just come out with a gun, just start shooting everything. And I'm getting hit. Everybody getting hit.

segments.speaker: Brandon Caro
segments.text: I would think what it would feel like to be blown up in an IED, to be pinned down, and have the vehicle set ablaze, and to burn alive, to be trapped in the truck because the doors were too heavy to cut through or to pull open.

segments.speaker: Curtis Jefferson
segments.text: Seeing it like this, seeing it with my own eyes, just look, seeing blood, and me just falling to the ground, and is too late for the ambulance? Would I still be alive when the ambulance come get me? Or that crazy kind of stuff, like, when you sit and think about that stuff, that kind of stuff drives you crazy.

segments.speaker: Alex Kotlowitz
segments.text: For both, reality eventually caught up to their fears. In the spring of 2006, Curtis told us he got caught in a shootout with rival drug dealers. The first bullet, to his back, spun him around. He got hit four more times, in the stomach and in the arm. As a result, he walks doubled over, like an old man. Because a permanent nerve damage, he falls a lot. And when he's under stress or eats the wrong food, he has bleeding from his intestines.

segments.speaker: Alex Kotlowitz
segments.text: Brandon, too, was hurt in a rollover when his Humvee fell off a small cliff. Brandon had been manning the turret, and fortunately, another soldier pulled him in just as the vehicle rolled. He suffered three fractures of his vertebrae and two herniated disks, and the pain kept him up nights, even after he left Afghanistan.

segments.speaker: Alex Kotlowitz
segments.text: Both men were on a lot of medications after their injuries. And our sixth similarity may not be so surprising-- they self-medicated.

segments.speaker: Brandon Caro
segments.text: I had started to drink again. And on the weekends, I would drink heavily.

segments.speaker: Curtis Jefferson
segments.text: It makes my body just feel a little better, like just a little basic, Mary Jane, that's all.

segments.speaker: Brandon Caro
segments.text: Usually a Crown and Coke was my drink of choice. And I would probably drink at least 5, up to 8, 9, 10 in the night.

segments.speaker: Curtis Jefferson
segments.text: But sometimes, it do give me the opposite effect.

segments.speaker: Brandon Caro
segments.text: When I was very, very drunk, I would start to cry because of how upset I was.

segments.speaker: Curtis Jefferson
segments.text: Because, you know, when I smoke, it put me on a mellow. Then, you know, you just start thinking. Then that's when all the thoughts just come, like, oh, what the hell they just come from? And I'd be like, oh, some thoughts I think sometimes, I don't want to think about.

segments.speaker: Alex Kotlowitz
segments.text: Echo number seven, they lashed out at friends and family. Curtis had night terrors, and would wake in the middle of the night thinking his girlfriend was someone who was trying to shoot him. He'd push her. He'd hit her in the head. He'd call her names.

segments.speaker: Curtis Jefferson
segments.text: I just was like, dang, I know I'm hurting this girl. I'm really putting my hands on her, like a man, putting marks on her arms. And I said, I'm losing it. And I was like, shh.

segments.speaker: Alex Kotlowitz
segments.text: Brandon had a difficult relationship with a girlfriend, too. They'd get into huge arguments and she'd get scared. One time, Brandon got so agitated, a friend intervened and tried to calm him down. Brandon punched him. His girlfriend locked herself in her room and called the police.

segments.speaker: Brandon Caro
segments.text: Police came. And I was inside. And the police rang the doorbell. And I opened it up. And it was two cops, a guy and a girl cop. And I asked the guy, is your weapon loaded? He said, why would you ask me something like that? I said, because I want you to shoot me in the head.

segments.speaker: Curtis Jefferson
segments.text: I was just sitting in my bedroom. And I had my gun under my bed, in a sneaker box. I had a 40 Mag, big, old cowboy gun. And that's when my grandma caught the gun in my mouth. Yeah, she just opened the door to make sure I was cool. It just was one of them days. She opened the door, and gun in my mouth, you know what I mean?

segments.speaker: Curtis Jefferson
segments.text: She didn't know what to do. She didn't know to come closer or stay back. She didn't know what to do. So she looking at me, start whooping and crying. And she didn't want to come next to me. And so she's just talking to me the whole time, like, come on, baby, it's all right, I love you. You're my grandson. You know, your mom ain't leave you out here on the Earth for this. You blessed. You just got shot five times. Why are you?

segments.speaker: Curtis Jefferson
segments.text: It's going to be all right. We're going to get some help for you and everything. And I just took it out, decocked it, put it back in the box, and just sat there. And called my homie up, and bring some weed around the corner, and got high. And that's how that went.

segments.speaker: Alex Kotlowitz
segments.text: Both Brandon and Curtis have gotten help. Brandon's in AA and went through a writing program for veterans at NYU. Curtis is receiving counseling through the program at Drexel that offers help to guys coming off the street. But finally, it's here where their stories diverge. Brandon's tour ended, and he's now thousands of miles from the dangers of Afghanistan. Curtis still lives in his old neighborhood, where the danger's ongoing.

segments.speaker: Curtis Jefferson
segments.text: When I get more money, I'm definitely moving. I'm going to move. That's a priority I'm working on right now. I'm out. I'm going to live somewhere comfortable, that I know I can walk in the neighborhood, I could sit out there on my step all day, all night, if I want to.

segments.speaker: Alex Kotlowitz
segments.text: Not long ago, a guy was shot and killed down the block from where he lives. And Curtis happened to see the body on the ground.

segments.speaker: Curtis Jefferson
segments.text: And I just was thinking about a lot of the-- I was paused. I just was like, yo, when he shot, like, damn, that boy was on the ground. And that was me. It's just, I'm living. Like, he died. And I'm like, damn. And it just felt like I felt all them bullets all over again.

segments.speaker: Alex Kotlowitz
segments.text: Curtis worries that because of the way he walks, perpetually bent over, he looks weak and that people will target him, rob him, beat him up, shoot him, take revenge. I wonder, for someone like Curtis, if it's really post-traumatic stress, since really, there's nothing post about it.

segments.speaker: Alex Kotlowitz
segments.text: Brandon, meanwhile, says he doesn't talk to his friends or family about his anger and his nightmares, which he still has regularly. He tried counseling, but didn't like it. So he sought out other veterans who understand what he's been through.

segments.speaker: Alex Kotlowitz
segments.text: And Curtis now attends group counseling with others who, like himself, were once running the streets. That's the final echo. They've both come to realize that they're not alone.
